newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark seen heading for 2.83 after pullback.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark seen heading for 2.83 after pullback.

text.p: Now that sterling has probed above 2.77 marks to its highest level in 53 months, technical analysts say its next major target is 2.83 and above, although they expect a slight pullback first.
Sterling scaled a peak of 2.7733 marks on Thursday, its best level since falling out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992, though it later slipped back below the key 2.77.

"Sterling/mark is basically trying to break out of an ascending triangle pattern. A break above 2.7705 would initially push sterling up to 2.7780," said Nick Shamin, analyst at Technical Data in London.

Although 2.7780 marks does not represent a special level on the charts, the market had earmarked it as a big psychological target amid sterling's recent rally because that was the level the currency was trading at when it crashed out of the ERM.

A triangle pattern dating back to February 19 has its base at 2.7015, sterling/mark's low that day, and has a horizontal resistance line at 2.7700. A culmination of this pattern upon a clear break above 2.77 would set up an implied medium-term target of 2.8385 marks.

"A break above 2.77 would mean a level from long ago, above 2.83, which is basically an area where there is a series of old lows way back at the beginning of 1992," said Marc Ostwald, technical analyst at London Bond Broking.

Karen Jones, technical analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston here, noted that the area above 2.8300 should be a good interim target as there were several lines of resistance between 2.8310 and 2.8365.
Some minor barriers would intervene before that, a key one being the psychological level of 2.80, she said.
"There are a quite a lot of things coming in at around 2.86 in the long term... My overall target is 2.85 to 2.86, which is a combination of Fibonacci retracements," Jones said.
She said 2.86 marks represented a 76.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the decline from 3.0575 in October 1990 to sterling's all-time low of 2.1683 marks, hit in November 1995.
However, the pound is expected to struggle for a while before heading in that direction.

"The problem is that sterling seems to have run out of steam, although there is a very good short-term trend. Looking at a wedge formation on the charts, it's ripe for a pullback," London Bond Broking's Ostwald said, adding that the wedge had a resistance line at 2.77 marks.
He said a correction would be in order especially if sterling failed to make a convincing break above that line, which he said was a level of massive congestion.

Such a correction, however, was expected to be fairly limited. A five-day moving average will underpin sterling at 2.7585 and after that, the rising base line of the triangle formation will provide major support at 2.7525, said Technical Data's Shamin.
